inputs.original_text: They’re trying to turn a political slogan into “profanity” so schools can suppress it without admitting they’re policing dissent. The phrase’s origin is right there: a crowd was shouting “F*** Joe Biden!” and an NBC interviewer recast it as “Let’s go Brandon!” Now lower courts say schools can ban clothing that “can reasonably be interpreted as profane”—a conveniently elastic rule that lets institutions decide which messages are acceptable. The brothers’ case is headed to the U.S. Supreme Court, and the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression says their First Amendment rights were violated. This looks less like a hoodie dispute than a test of how far officials can stretch a label to silence speech they don’t want heard.
inputs.modified_text:
They’ve found a neat way to make political dissent disappear: call it “profanity,” then let schools claim they’re just enforcing a rule. The “Let’s go Brandon!” wording didn’t erase what the crowd meant when it shouted “F*** Joe Biden!”—it just gave institutions a softer label to work with. And now “can reasonably be interpreted as profane” is elastic enough to put officials in charge of deciding which messages are allowed.

The brothers’ case heading to the U.S. Supreme Court matters because this isn’t really about a hoodie. It’s about whether schools can stretch a vague standard until it serves as a tool for suppressing speech they dislike. The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression says their First Amendment rights were violated; the broader pattern looks like dissent being repackaged as misconduct so the people enforcing the rules can pretend it isn’t political.
